To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. passages.text: Training large language models (LLMs) entails a fundamental trade-off: memory-efficient optimizers such as Adam discard cross-parameter curvature, whereas full-curvature methods such as SOAP can accelerate convergence at prohibitive memory costs. We introduce Clean , a memory-efficient and full-curvature optimizer designed to resolve this bottleneck. Clean leverages the randomized Nyström method to accurately approximate the left and right preconditioners in SOAP, and to reduce the optimizer’s memory complexity from quadratic to linear in terms of model dimensions. We subsequently reintegrate the off-subspace components to capture curvature information beyond the low-rank approximation, preserving rich curvature at minimal memory cost. We further propose Q-Clean , a low-precision variant that aggressively compresses optimizer states. Q-Clean reduces optimizer memory consumption by over 50% compared to Muon when pre-training a LLaMA-1.3B architecture, all while maintaining strong and competitive predictive performance. Notably, Clean operates with a smaller optimizer-state footprint than standard AdamW while reaching AdamW’s final performance 26% faster in wall-clock time. Furthermore, our methods uniquely enable the pre-training of a 13B-parameter model on a single 80GB GPU, providing a scalable, efficient, and accessible approach to large-scale model optimization. $*$ $*$ footnotetext: Equal contribution.

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the bottleneck rank , rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features. 0 0 footnotetext: ⋆ Corresponding author.

Fine-tuning large pretrained models on downstream tasks is effective but expensive: updating all parameters of a billion-scale model requires substantial memory and compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) solves this problem by adapting a large pretrained model while updating only a small subset of parameters. Some of the representative approaches include adapter modules ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , prefix tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ) , prompt tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022 ). Among these, LoRA stands out as an attractive option because it keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and modifies selected linear maps by adding trainable low-rank updates. More formally, for a weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as W = W 0 + T , T = U ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ m × r , V ∈ ℝ n × r , W=W_{0}+T,\qquad T=UV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, The rank r r is typically chosen by the practitioner as a hyperparameter rather than something derived from the fine-tuning objective itself ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Schulman and Lab, 2025 ) . A fundamental theoretical question is therefore: When does the regularized fine-tuning objective itself admit a low-rank global minimizer, and what controls the rank?

Our answer starts with a simple observation: once the backbone is frozen, the loss does not observe an adapted matrix T T directly, but only through a finite-rank linear map determined by the frozen activations. Concretely, if H = [ h 1 , … , h N ] H=[h_{1},\ldots,h_{N}] is the matrix of frozen input features across the N N training samples, the empirical loss depends on T T only through the product T ​ H TH . We call rank ⁡ ( Φ ) \rank(\Phi) , where Φ ⁡ ( T ) = T ​ H \Phi(T)=TH , the bottleneck rank of the adapted block. The same principle applies blockwise to multiple adapted stages and attention heads. Trace-norm regularization then selects a low-rank representative among all matrices that induce the same observed output. This yields exact low-rank existence results without linearizing the network around the pretrained weights. For multi-head attention ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) , the same principle becomes sharper because attention introduces additional invariances: row-wise softmax is unchanged by additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and the frozen output projection. passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

We express effective matrix dynamics through the layer updates and derive an exact mode reduction under explicit balance and alignment assumptions. The reduction separates the contribution of the factorization from the optimizer update states.

( 𝟐 ) \mathbf{(2)} Phase laws revealing how optimizer settings shape the bias of depth. We derive birth, saturation, and decay laws that distinguish normalization, accumulated history, and damping. GD and SignGD dynamics establish contrasting reference behaviors. Instantaneous Adam identifies how a positive stabilizer restores slow dynamics at small gradient magnitudes. Ideal Muon accelerates both emergence and removal of modes in finite time. For cumulative Shampoo, an exact accumulator identity quantifies the transition from initialization dominated to history dominated dynamics. For the specified K-FAC block model, an exact birth time decomposition separates an undamped contribution from a damping-weighted GD contribution. Together, these results identify when optimizer geometry preserves, modifies, or cancels the suppression of small modes induced by depth. ( 𝟑 ) \mathbf{(3)} Numerical validation of phase laws and regime transitions. Controlled experiments in deep matrix factorization and regression verify the derived phase laws. These experiments demonstrate that settings commonly associated with numerical stability can change relative spectral progress, determining which components emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

Our analysis shows that the spectral bias of depth depends on optimizer geometry and the stage of training. A surprising consequence is that rapid learning of weak components can coexist with rapid removal of unsupported ones, as illustrated by the Muon analysis. Conversely, accumulated history can accelerate the emergence of a mode while prolonging its persistence. These effects make a single ordering of optimizers by stronger or weaker low-rank bias inadequate. A further implication is that parameters associated with numerical stability also shape learning bias. In the analyzed models, Adam’s stabilizer, Shampoo’s accumulator initialization, and K-FAC’s damping determine where normalization, history, or curvature correction governs spectral progress. They can therefore change how strongly depth suppresses small modes, even within the same optimizer. Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior. This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

This is a direct precedent for connecting geometry to motion outside the observed coordinates. Our block curvature analysis quantifies the effect of additive damping on mode birth and decay, and distinguishes it from both full curvature and factored damping. These works provide important geometry and momentum precedents, while our phase laws concern squared loss, explicit stabilization or damping factors, and finite targets in factorized models.

GD and SignGD dynamics establish contrasting reference behaviors. Instantaneous Adam identifies how a positive stabilizer restores slow dynamics at small gradient magnitudes. Ideal Muon accelerates both emergence and removal of modes in finite time. For cumulative Shampoo, an exact accumulator identity quantifies the transition from initialization dominated to history dominated dynamics. For the specified K-FAC block model, an exact birth time decomposition separates an undamped contribution from a damping-weighted GD contribution. Together, these results identify when optimizer geometry preserves, modifies, or cancels the suppression of small modes induced by depth. Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. Conversely, accumulated history can accelerate the emergence of a mode while prolonging its persistence. These effects make a single ordering of optimizers by stronger or weaker low-rank bias inadequate. A further implication is that parameters associated with numerical stability also shape learning bias. Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior. This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

passages.section: A.1 Memory Savings Do Not Guarantee Lower Inference Latency
passages.text: We compare dense inference with the unstructured SLR representation used by SALAAD on a synthetic Llama-1B MLP down projection of size × 5632 2048\!\times\!5632 . The benchmark uses a 15 % 15\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} rank ratio and 5 % 5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} nonzero density, with the sparse component stored as a PyTorch torch.sparse_csr_tensor . Both representations are profiled on a Quadro RTX 6000 with batch size 128 and sequence length 256. As shown in Figure 7 , static weight memory falls from 23.07 MB 23.07\text{\,}\mathrm{MB} to 10.49 MB 10.49\text{\,}\mathrm{MB} , a 54.5 % 54.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} reduction, while throughput falls to 2.68 % 2.68\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of the dense reference. For this fixed workload, the throughput ratio implies a projection inference latency 37.3 37.3 times that of the dense baseline. Unstructured sparse components incur indexing and irregular memory-access overheads that can offset the computational savings from sparsity ( Mishra et al., 2021 ) . This example illustrates why reduced weight storage alone does not ensure efficient inference. passages.text: Synergy with post-training compression. Applying SliceGPT and SVD-LLM to L L -only checkpoints pretrained with S-SALAAD yields lower perplexity at the same inference cost than applying them to vanilla-pretrained checkpoints. This benefit persists on both GPU and CPU (Figures 23(a) and 24(a) ), demonstrating that the learned compressibility remains useful across hardware. Block granularity and deployment trade-offs. On Llama-1B, the × 16 16\!\times\!16 variant achieves lower perplexity than L L -only under tight compression budgets (Figure 6(b) ). Its additional inference overhead, however, limits the deployment gains on both GPU and CPU (Figures 23(a) and 24(a) ). Increasing the block size reduces this overhead, allowing × 64 64\!\times\!64 to closely track the L L -only perplexity–memory–latency trade-offs on the RTX 2080 Ti and improve on them at CPU operating points. These trends support the conclusion that retaining S S can improve deployment trade-offs beyond L L -only when block granularity is matched to the target hardware, as further illustrated in Appendix G .

passages.text: Figure 26 extends the analysis in Section 5.2 by comparing the deployment trade-offs of different block granularities and the L L -only special case across model scales and hardware. (a) Llama-350M, Quadro RTX 6000. (b) Llama-1B, Quadro RTX 6000. (c) Llama-1B, RTX 2080 Ti. (d) Llama-1B, CPU. Figure 26: Perplexity against throughput on Llama for different block granularities, including the L L -only baseline. Marker radius encodes peak GPU memory with min–max scaling or peak RAM with proportional scaling, per panel. Finer blocks better preserve quality under tight compression budgets, but their additional inference overhead limits the deployment gains. On Llama-350M, coarser blocks incur a pronounced quality penalty despite their higher throughput (Figure 26(a) ). On Llama-1B, the coarsest blocks retain competitive quality and closely track the L L -only deployment trade-offs on both GPUs (Figures 26(b) and 26(c) ). On CPU, the same granularity also provides operating points that improve on L L -only (Figure 26(d) ). passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. Under controlled settings, we compare CORE with two recent state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, Tongyi DeepResearch ( Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2025 ) and OpenResearcher ( Li et al., 2026b ) , on BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , BrowseComp-Wikipedia ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus CM ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) . To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

CORE achieves the highest answer accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark group, producing new state-of-the-art results. On BrowseComp-Plus, it improves both metrics over the stronger baseline, OpenResearcher, for all three agent models. The gains are largest for Qwen3.8-27B, at 6.39 points in accuracy and 7.40 points in recall. On BrowseComp-Wikipedia, CORE keeps its lead across all three agents. With GPT-5.4, it improves both metrics by more than eight points over OpenResearcher. Higher accuracy therefore comes with broader coverage of the annotated relevant documents in both the web and Wikipedia corpora. See some case studies in Appendix C .

We presented CORE , a training-free deep research harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves whole passages to judge relevance, then reuses the reranker’s token-level similarities to return only the most relevant snippet from each one. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. Across three agent models and three benchmarks, CORE achieves higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher in every model–benchmark comparison, while returning substantially fewer tokens per search than Tongyi DeepResearch. passages.text: Yueran Ma Affiliation: The University of Queensland Affiliation: Brisbane, Australia Email: s4931778@student.uq.edu.au

Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/lora-second-descent-C7B5 .

LoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) builds on intrinsic-dimension measurements of objective landscapes ( Li et al., 2018 ; Aghajanyan et al., 2021 ) ; its rank expressivity is characterized by Zeng & Lee (2024) and its scaling conventions by Kalajdzievski (2023) . That large ranks can hurt is established: accuracy stagnates past ranks of 32 32 – 64 64 ( Jung et al., 2025 ) , optima are task-dependent ( Rathore et al., 2025 ) , LoRA “learns less and forgets less” ( Biderman et al., 2024 ) , and low-rank updates memorize less in large language models ( Bossy et al., 2026 ) ; in noisy-label classification, Kim et al. (2024) find that the capacity limit of PEFT also impedes learning clean examples. Under label noise, theory places the optimal rank lower as noise grows ( Steele, 2026 ) and accuracy degrades with rank when noise is strong ( Zindari et al., 2026 ) , while Park (2026) and Rushka & Klabjan (2026) analyze rank sufficiency and approximation error. Empirically, Dennis et al. (2026) find ranks 16 16 to 128 128 all trailing full fine-tuning and Albert et al. (2025) ask whether the shortfall is parameters or rank, neither under label noise. These establish the two endpoints. What remains unmeasured is the shape between them, where risk peaks relative to the rank at which optimization interpolates, and whether the post-peak branch recovers once the adapter can express any dense update.

Effective capacity and optimization geometry. That LoRA’s update carries a stable rank well below its nominal rank is likewise established, as a pathology to engineer away ( Lion et al., 2025 ) and as a sweep locating where validation accuracy turns ( Awofeso et al., 2025 ) ; we add its placement relative to interpolation and an intervention on it. Parameterization matters beyond expressivity ( Shuttleworth et al., 2025 ) , and learning rate interacts with rank through initialization and scaling ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , which is why the shared-rate sweep is checked against per-arm rates (each at its own rate) on every backbone (Section 5.3 , Appendices C.2 and C.3 ). The optimization geometry of the factored parameterization is mapped: freezing one factor ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2024 ) or both ( Kopiczko et al., 2024 ) , preconditioning the gradient ( Zhang & Pilanci, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Ghosh et al., 2026 ) , and showing that different factorizations of one Δ ​ W \Delta W converge differently ( Castin et al., 2026 ; Oh et al., 2026 ) . Those results concern training and generalization of the factorization; ours concern where the post-peak branch reaches dense risk (Section 5.3 ). Chang et al. (2025) use “double descent” for a transient training-loss divergence, a different object. Memorization and calibration under noise. Interpolating noisy labels forces memorization ( Zhang et al., 2017 ; Feldman & Zhang, 2020 ) , and calibration itself depends on overparameterization in high-dimensional models ( Clarté et al., 2023 ) , which is why we separate the risk we measure from the temperature it is read at (Section 5.6 ).

The parameter effective rank depends on the part of the update that changes the spectrum, meaning the part aligned with the parameter’s own singular basis, and how concentrated it is in the leading directions of this basis. Figure 5 (b) shows this directly: the top targeted and AdamW curves peak at the leading directions, while Muon and the bottom arm stay near uniform. Our optimizer extends recent matrix optimizers for full-parameter training to the manifold of fixed-rank matrices by interpreting them as normalization under a rotated basis. We show how rotation and normalization can be integrated with the fixed-rank manifold efficiently. Our optimizer converges faster to lower held-out loss and achieves better or comparable downstream performance on both supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks.

Large language models (LLMs) based on the transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) have achieved remarkable success in recent years ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . These models typically adopt a pretraining-finetuning paradigm, where large-scale pretraining equips a model with general capabilities and subsequent finetuning adapts it to specific downstream applications. However, as LLMs grow to billions of parameters, full-parameter finetuning becomes expensive in both computation and memory. Such a challenge has motivated the development of parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , which only update a small fraction of all parameters. Among these approaches, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) has emerged as a particularly effective method and has been widely adopted. LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and parametrizes the weight updates as products of low-rank matrices, substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters and the memory footprint, while maintaining competitive performance. Compared with full-parameter training, LoRA exhibits a unique geometric structure induced by its low-rank factorization. Specifically, the low-rank matrices have infinitely many reparameterizations that represent the same weight update, since the model’s output depends on these low-rank factors only through their product. This invariance, commonly referred to as gauge symmetry, suggests that optimization should respect the underlying geometry of the weight space of the LoRA parametrization. Motivated by this observation, we revisit the optimization of LoRA and aim to explicitly incorporate its gauge symmetry into the design of the optimization algorithm.

We design our optimizer on the manifold of fixed-rank matrices, aiming to optimize the product of the low-rank factors directly rather than each factor separately. We extend the recent advances in matrix optimizers ( Gong et al., 2026 ; Jordan et al., 2024 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) to the fixed-rank manifold by interpreting their update rules as normalization under a rotated basis. Our optimizer applies row and column normalization in a conditioning frame defined by the left singular vectors of the tangent momentum, projects the resulting direction back onto the tangent space, and retracts to the fixed-rank manifold. By exploiting the low-rank structure of tangent vectors, all operations can be performed using thin factors without materializing full weight-sized matrices. We refer to our proposed optimizer as RoM ( Ro tated M anifold Optimization). We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks. RoM achieves substantially lower held-out loss and better or comparable downstream task performance compared with other LoRA optimizers, with only modest additional computational overhead.

We further evaluate RoM on LoRA-based RL finetuning using the VeRL framework ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) . Since the other LoRA baselines do not specify an RL training recipe, we focus on comparing RoM against Adam. We train the Qwen2.5-3B base model ( Yang et al., 2024 ) using GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) on the training split of MATH (7.5K problems) with rank r = 16 r=16 . At each rollout step, we sample 8 responses for each of 128 prompts, yielding 1024 sequences per optimization step. We use no KL penalty and train for 400 steps. Following the setup of Liu et al. (2025) , we use the bare questions as prompts with no chat template. We evaluate the finetuned model using greedy decoding on three held-out benchmarks: MATH-500 (500 examples), GSM8K test (1319 examples), and OlympiadBench ( He et al., 2024 ) (674 examples). We tune Adam’s learning rate on a logarithmic grid and select 3 × 10 − 6 3\times 10^{-6} . We use the same learning rate for RoM without further tuning. By exploiting the low-rank structure of tangent vectors, RoM enables efficient Riemannian optimization with memory requirement comparable to conventional LoRA optimization. Ablation experiments further show that both normalization and rotation contribute to its optimization performance.

passages.text: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? This objective is not equivalent to the quality of a general research report. We introduce Idea2Prior, an extension of PaperArena and its implementation [ 1 , 2 ] . The contribution is an engineering and evaluation framework for inspectable idea-to-paper retrieval: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking. This makes it possible to distinguish a discovery miss from a candidate that was retrieved but lost during filtering, or from a task that failed operationally. A high-level result alone cannot make those distinctions.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

2. A retrieval-only execution mode that preserves abstract and PDF evidence assessment while omitting report-specific processing, exposed through local web, Python, CLI, and Notebook interfaces. 3. A three-system historical evaluation with explicit target-recovery, agreement, latency, token, and cost accounting, together with preserved prompts and outputs. 4. Optional implementation-analysis, citation-evolution, planning, benchmark-landscape, and citation-gap extensions, with their earlier exploratory evaluations distinguished from the retrieval benchmark.

evidence.quote: Across LLaMA models with $124$M to $500$M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss.

Figure 2 shows the post-training fragility that motivates this work: Muon falls to 5.72 % 5.72\% test accuracy after only 30 % 30\% MLP-channel pruning. Muon+GL remains robust through 50 % 50\% pruning, while NuMuon degrades more gradually under low-rank compression. Under magnitude-based pruning, BMuon is substantially more compressible than the structured baselines while matching Muon’s dense accuracy: BMuon reaches 71.46 % 71.46\% , versus 71.49 % 71.49\% for Muon, 71.25 % 71.25\% for Muon+GL, and 69.95 % 69.95\% for NuMuon. Using μ \mu for ranking provides a further gain: at 80 % 80\% pruning, BM- μ \mu retains 70.57 % 70.57\% accuracy, compared with 60.84 % 60.84\% for BM-mag, while Muon, Muon+GL, and NuMuon have fallen to 1.93 % 1.93\% , 6.01 % 6.01\% , and 3.84 % 3.84\% , respectively. The advantage of BM-mag under the shared magnitude criterion isolates the compressibility benefit of BMuon training, while the further gain from BM- μ \mu indicates that the learned allocation also carries useful channel-importance information.

The BMuon construction on MLP hidden channels extends naturally to gated MLPs such as SwiGLU, as used in LLaMA-style models. BMuon uses α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and K = 0.2 ​ N K=0.2N . After training, we globally prune SwiGLU hidden channels without recovery, using weight magnitude and an activation-aware score combining root-mean-square activation and output-weight norm; for BMuon, we also rank channels by μ \mu . In contrast, BMuon preserves its unpruned performance up to 80 % 80\% pruning, reaching 12.86 12.86 with activation ranking and 12.85 12.85 with μ \mu ranking. BMuon substantially outperforms Muon when both use the same magnitude or activation criterion at moderate and high pruning levels, while μ \mu again provides an effective pruning score. Overall, BMuon trades some unpruned quality for substantially greater robustness to structured channel pruning.
